desc:
The non-empty arrays a and b are each sorted in non-decreasing order. Choose one element from each array, and let s be their sum. Return the smallest possible value of |s - target|.

a = [-3, 4, 10, 20]
b = [1, 6, 15]
target = 17
result = 1

The closest sums to 17 are 10 + 6 = 16 (distance 1) and 4 + 15 = 19 (distance 2), so the answer is 1.
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Trying all pairs takes n · m steps. Use the sorted order to discard whole rows or columns of the implicit table of sums.
Put i at the start of a and j at the end of b. Look at the sum a[i] + b[j]. If it is below the target, which of the two pointers is it pointless to keep using with the current partner?
Record |sum - target| every step. If the sum is smaller than the target move i right; if larger move j left; if equal the answer is 0.
editorial: Imagine the table of all sums with row i and column j; it is sorted along every row and column. Start in the corner (0, m-1). If a[i] + b[j] < target, then every other sum in row i to the left of this one is even smaller, so they are all farther from the target than this one on the same side: row i is finished and i moves right. If the sum exceeds the target, the same argument shows that column j is finished (everything below it is larger), so j moves left.

At each visited cell record the distance to the target and keep the minimum. The pointers sweep monotonically, so there are at most n + m steps: O(n + m) time and O(1) space. Bounds on the values keep |s - target| within 2·109, inside 32 bits.
